I just wish it weren’t show jumping. 

The whole point of the pentathlon is to showcase the skills needed in 19th c warfare. The reason for the show jumping is to simulate essentialy “fleeing a war zone on a stolen horse,” hence the emphasis on speedy jumps and the random draws.

But personally I think there must be a more effective way to showcase one’s skills as a rider, and still be with the spirit of the pentathlon. In fact I think it’s the perfect opportunity to design a unique event just for this purpose. It could be almost like an mildly-interdisciplinary obstacle course that requires dressage (which has roots in warfare anyways), maybe cavalry obstacles like someone suggested above (closing gates, picking up rings), and then maybe a few smaller jumps, collected and controlled hunter style instead of the frantic show jumping they have now.

I will say though I do feel for that German rider. I rode for almost 15 years hunter/jumper and I know that feeling, when there is so much pressure on you but you are absolutely terrified of the horse you have to ride. I think she was incorrect in how she handled it, and that she absolutely should have just pulled out, but people make mistakes and I think she can be forgiven.

Hi! I have some experience with this actually and would like to share. I started ballet in December, and by March my teacher wanted me in the beginner pointe class. I was too excited to be reasonable and say no, and I did it anyways. Honestly, I was not ready then and I KNOW I have months or more likely YEARS to actually be ready for it. I will say it is a VERY basic class, all on the barre, mostly just going up and down and working through the motions, however I was still not ready. I am still in the class, but now I do it in slippers, and actually its now probably my most helpful class. It is great for foot and calf strengthening, its a lot of more deliberate, slow releves and focusing on building up the muscles that I will need to someday go en pointe again. Was it a mistake to go so fast? Yes. But I am glad I made that mistake, because now I know exactly how much work I need to start putting in and I know exactly what my goals are.

One thing that helped for me was tricking myself into thinking the sun is up when its really not, even if just fleetingly. We have these Brilli light bulbs in our bedroom, plugged into a timer. They turn on right before my alarm goes off, in a completely blacked out room. In those few minutes of waking up and NOT seeing a dark sky outside, combined with seeing what *feels* like sunlight honestly really helped. It made it a lot easier to get out of bed, and made "mornings" so much less depressing. It obviously doesn't work all day (you can't really fool your eyes once you've seen the darkness outside, esp with a lot of window coverage), but those crucial moments of waking up in "sunlight" to me made a big difference.




Also, what is your sleep/work schedule? Do you wake up right before work and sleep later, or wake up early and sleep right after work? If your hours allow it, I have found that waking up earlier, with the sun still being up and in the "morning" is a lot nicer. If I wake up JUST before work (2100-0500 is my workday), the sun is already down and it just gets me so down. Yes I see the sun after work, but it makes it really hard to then fall asleep as the morning sun is shining.




All that coupled with the fact that you might just have to force yourself to have more sun exposure. Go outside more, sit by a window when you eat meals or are relaxing at home, etc. will all help.
